title: The twisting rhythm after a new antibiotic
note: Fictional patient. Doses and energies are quoted from the 2025 AHA guidelines (and the ERC where named) for recognition; your unit protocol, crash-cart stock and the attending nephrologist come first. Simulation success is an educational result, not a prediction of patient survival.
intro: Saturday, 10:20 a.m. Mrs. Lorna Bautista, 67, dialyzes through a left-arm fistula on a 2 mmol/L potassium bath; her potassium before the session was 4.0. Three days ago another clinic started azithromycin for a cough. Three hours into the session she says her heart “raced and skipped” for a few seconds and she felt dizzy. The monitor memory shows a 6-second run of fast, wide complexes that twist around the baseline, then sinus rhythm again. She is alert; pressure 118/70. You are her dialysis nurse.

choices.text: Stop fluid removal, call the physician-on-duty, pads on, 12-lead ECG, send electrolytes.
choices.feedback: A run of polymorphic VT that stops by itself is a warning, not a reassurance: the next run may not stop. Stop fluid removal, put the pads on, get a 12-lead to look at the QT, send potassium, magnesium and calcium, and give the physician the results and the full medicine list, including drugs started outside the unit.

choices.text: Chart the run and recheck her in 15 minutes, since it stopped by itself and she is alert and talking now.
choices.feedback: Self-terminating polymorphic VT often comes back and can become sustained.
choices.then: Four minutes later another run makes her dizzy; you stop fluid removal and call the physician-on-duty.

choices.text: Ask for adenosine to stop the fast runs before they come back, since she is stable and has a pulse now.
choices.feedback: Adenosine is for stable, regular, narrow-complex tachycardia. It does not treat polymorphic VT, and between runs she is in sinus rhythm.
choices.then: The physician-on-duty arrives, stops the order and asks for a 12-lead.

n2.scene: The 12-lead shows sinus rhythm 56 with a long QT; the machine reads the QTc as 590 ms. Blood gas potassium: 3.1 mmol/L. Short twisting runs keep coming and going; between them she is alert, 112/68.
n2.prompt: You are the physician-on-duty. Which plan fits?

choices.text: Magnesium per protocol, correct the potassium, stop the azithromycin, call the attending.
choices.feedback: Recurrent polymorphic VT with a long QT is torsades de pointes. Magnesium may be considered (AHA 2025, COR 2b, LOE C-LD). Low potassium after a low-potassium bath and a QT-prolonging antibiotic are the likely triggers: correct the potassium per protocol and stop the drug. Keep the pads on. The dose and whether the session continues are the physician’s and the attending nephrologist’s decision.

choices.text: Amiodarone IV to suppress the runs, since it treats ventricular tachycardia and she still has a pulse.
choices.feedback: Amiodarone lengthens the QT. AHA 2025 lists amiodarone or lidocaine for recurrent polymorphic VT only when the QT is not prolonged.
choices.then: The attending nephrologist, on the phone, asks you to hold it and give magnesium instead.

choices.text: Finish her fluid goal on the same 2 mmol/L potassium bath, then treat the rhythm after she comes off.
choices.feedback: Dialyzing against a low-potassium bath lowers her potassium further, which can provoke more torsades. The bath and the session are now the attending’s decision.
choices.then: The attending stops the session plan and asks for the potassium to be corrected first.

vitals.ecg: Sinus 56, long QT (QTc 590 ms); runs of polymorphic VT

n3.scene: During the next run she slumps. No response, no normal breathing, no pulse. The twisting rhythm does not stop.

choices.text: CPR, stop the blood pump, and an unsynchronized shock as soon as it is charged.
choices.feedback: Pulseless polymorphic VT is treated like VF. Sustained polymorphic VT needs an immediate unsynchronized shock (AHA 2025, COR 1, LOE B-NR); the machine cannot synchronize to these twisting complexes.

vitals.rhythmLabel: Sinus rhythm 64, long QT, pulse present

choices.text: Synchronized cardioversion, because she was in VT with a pulse only a moment ago and sync is safer.
choices.feedback: She has no pulse now, and sync cannot find reliable R waves in torsades: the device may not fire, and the delay costs time.
choices.then: The defibrillator will not discharge in sync; you switch sync off and shock.

vitals.rhythmLabel: Sinus rhythm 64, long QT, pulse present

choices.text: Give the magnesium first and wait a minute to see whether it stops the rhythm before shocking.
choices.feedback: The shock comes first. Magnesium does not replace defibrillation, and routine magnesium in cardiac arrest is not recommended (AHA 2025, COR 3: No Benefit).
choices.then: The leader calls for the shock; 90 seconds have passed.

vitals.rhythmLabel: Sinus rhythm 66, long QT, pulse present

n4.scene: After one shock: pulse and pressure are back, 96/58, sinus rhythm 64. The QT is still long.

choices.text: Pads on, monitor, recheck potassium and magnesium, flag the drug, transfer for monitored care.
choices.feedback: ROSC care plus removing the triggers: keep the pads on and record azithromycin as a QT warning in her chart. The QT is still long, so torsades can return. She needs a monitored bed and a review of every QT-prolonging medicine, including those started outside the unit; tell the clinic that prescribed it.

choices.text: Restart dialysis to finish her fluid goal, now that she has a pulse and her pressure is acceptable.
choices.feedback: After an arrest, the session decision belongs to the attending nephrologist, and the low-potassium bath helped cause this.
choices.then: The attending ends the session and arranges transfer.

end.title: 11:15 a.m.
end.text: Mrs. Bautista is transferred to a monitored bed with both 12-lead ECGs, the recorder’s sheet and a note that azithromycin was stopped. The prescribing clinic is informed.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • A self-terminating run of twisting VT is a warning: stop fluid removal, pads on, 12-lead, electrolytes, full drug list.
  • Long QT plus recurrent polymorphic VT is torsades: magnesium may be considered (COR 2b); correct potassium; stop QT-prolonging drugs. Amiodarone and lidocaine are for polymorphic VT with a normal QT.
  • No pulse, or sustained polymorphic VT: immediate unsynchronized shock; sync cannot lock on. No routine magnesium in arrest.
  • The dialysis link: a low-potassium bath, low magnesium and new QT-prolonging drugs (some antibiotics, antifungals and antiemetics) add up.
